signals.title: Buoyant Releases Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for Kubernetes and vLLM - MarkTechPost
signals.excerpt:
# Buoyant Releases Kinference: An Open Source Inference Control Plane for Kubernetes and vLLM

By

Michal Sutter

November 7, 2026

Buoyant, the company behind Linkerd, has released Kinference, an open source project for building inference platforms on Kubernetes. Kinference is an inference control plane for Kubernetes and vLLM. It sits in front of a fleet of vLLM workers and decides where each request goes. It applies routing policies, token rate limits, KV-cache-aware load balancing and per-tenant metrics in one layer. For dev teams serving many open-weight models to many internal clients, it targets the layer above the model server. The project is Apache 2.0 licensed on GitHub. The current release is v0.1.0-alpha.7.

## TL;DR

- Size: v0.1.0-alpha.7, written in Rust, Apache 2.0, configured through 5 Kubernetes CRDs.
- Runs on: any GPU-enabled Kubernetes cluster running vLLM. Buoyant’s benchmark used 3 L40S GPUs per pool.
- Performance: large gains on prefix-heavy traffic versus plain Kubernetes Service routing (self-reported).
- Best: median TTFT fell from 6.88 s to 0.31 s (95%) on a shared-prefix workload.
- Worst: no median TTFT gain on prompts without shared prefixes (6.92 s vs 6.83 s).

...

## How fast is Kinference in benchmarks?

Buoyant published a benchmark against plain Kubernetes load balancing. Each arm used 3 vLLM 0.31.0 pods, each on 1 L40S GPU. The model was Qwen3.8-27B-FP8. Load came from GuideLLM 0.8.1. The baseline was a ClusterIP Service, where kube-proxy picks a random pod per connection.

Unloaded latency results (median TTFT):

| Workload | Kubernetes Service | Kinference | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Control (no shared prefix) | 6.92 s | 6.83 s | No significant difference |
| Shared-prefix | 6.88 s | 0.31 s | about -95% |
| Multiturn | 1.70 s | 0.59 s | about -65% |

Median end-to-end latency fell 45% on shared-prefix and 32% on multiturn. On control traffic, p95 TTFT still dropped from 21.46 s to 12.33 s. Buoyant attributes this to queue-aware balancing.

The capacity test measured goodput: requests per minute meeting a TTFT SLO. Peak goodput was 103.0 vs 14.0 req/min on shared-prefix, about 7.4x. On multiturn it was 82.7 vs 23.8, about 3.5x. The Service baseline never met the SLO at any tested concurrency.

These numbers are self-reported. The baseline is random routing, not another cache-aware router like llm-d or Dynamo. Buoyant also notes its SLOs (8 s and 4 s) suit offline agents, not chat.

signals.title: Speed Up Image Generation with FLUX 3 Image Klein on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs | NVIDIA Technical Blog
signals.excerpt:
- FLUX 3 Image Klein Base and its distilled variant combine Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct for text conditioning, a diffusion transformer, and an autoencoder to generate and edit images at high resolution.
- TensorRT LLM VisualGen accelerates inference on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with NVFP4 quantization, fused PrimsTS GEMM kernels, and torch.compile, delivering up to 1.62x faster text-to-image and 1.58x faster image-to-image generation over BF16 on a single B200.
- Quantized attention options include cuDNN FP8 and VC-Attention FP8; VC-Attention FP8 with a repair budget of 0.005 achieved 1.18x speedups for both Base and distilled models at 2048x2048 with LPIPS scores of 0.086 and 0.151.
- Sol-Attention sparse attention with τ=1.0 and 12 initial dense steps provided 1.30x faster denoising plus decoding for Base, while 16 dense steps prioritized fidelity at 1.24x.
- Cache-DiT step caching nearly halved Base latency at both 1024x1024 and 2048x2048, reaching 1.94x speedup at the higher resolution with an LPIPS of 0.033.
- Multi-GPU scaling with CFG and Ulysses parallelism on eight B200 GPUs reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and from 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled, with denoising speedups of 6.01x and 4.44x.

...

FLUX 3 Image Klein is an image editing and generation model from Black Forest Labs (BFL) trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA GPUs. It offers Base and distilled checkpoints for different latency and fidelity requirements.

This tutorial shows how to configure FLUX 3 Image Klein in NVIDIA TensorRT LLM VisualGen to take advantage of fused kernels, multi-GPU parallelism, FP8/NVFP4 support, caching, and attention optimizations. It compares latency and changes in generated outputs across optimizations. In the reported 2048×2048 tests on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU, combined optimizations delivered up to 3.46x faster text-to-image (T2I) and 4.45x faster image-to-image (I2I) generation for FLUX 3 Image Klein Base compared with uncompiled BF16 inference. The tutorial includes deployment instructions and YAML configurations for applying these optimizations to your workloads.

...

At 2048×2048, scaling from one to eight GPUs on an NVIDIA DGX B200 reduced median T2I latency from 14.90 to 3.00 seconds for Base and 2.73 to 1.08 seconds for distilled. Denoising speedups were larger, at 6.01x for Base and 4.44x for distilled Klein, but roughly half of eight-GPU distilled generation time remained outside denoising, limiting end-to-end gains.

...

On a single B200, compilation, NVFP4 with PrimsTS GEMMs, Sol-Attention, and Cache-DiT delivered a 3.46x generation speedup for T2I, reducing latency from 22.36 to 6.46 seconds, and a 4.45x speedup for I2I, reducing latency from 54.64 to 12.28 seconds. The 16-step distilled Klein achieved up to 2.34x end-to-end speedups.

...

### Online serving endpoint

From the same container directory, launch the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/images/generations` endpoint:

```
cd /app/tensorrt_llm/examples/visual_gen
trtllm-serve black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --visual_gen_args configs/flux3-images-1gpu.yaml

```

Once the server is ready, open a second terminal, enter the running container, and run the client:

```
docker exec -it tensorrt_llm bash
python examples/visual_gen/serve/sync_image_gen.py \
  --base-url http://localhost:8000/v1 \
  --model black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base \
  --size 2048x2048 \
  --prompt "A small robot tending a rooftop garden at sunrise" \
  --output flux3-served.png

```

signals.title: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Logs 848 Tokens per Second per Agent on GB300 NVL72 | TokenPost
signals.excerpt:
# DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Logs 848 Tokens per Second per Agent on GB300 NVL72

A reading about a month earlier was 596 tokens per second per agent on the same rack. The figure measures one session’s output pace, not total system throughput.

By Simon Yoon

Published Nov 8, 2026, 2:33 PM EST

A GPU compute tray under a hard overhead light / TokenPost.ai (mono)

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash produced 848 tokens a second for one agent on Nvidia’s GB300 NVL72, up 252 over roughly a month on the same setup, a change relevant to AI capacity planning.

The earlier reading was 596 tokens per second per agent. The rack setup remained the same, while the broader performance work involves model design, serving software and hardware; the comparison does not isolate the contribution of each.

Per-agent decoding speed measures how quickly one session generates output. Aggregate throughput totals output across a system, so the two measures describe different scales of activity.

V4.1 Flash is a multimodal mixture-of-experts model with 552 billion parameters in total. It activates 16 billion parameters during decoding, when it generates a response, and accepts text and image inputs. Its context window extends to 1 million tokens.

Nvidia’s GB300 NVL72 places 72 GPUs in a single rack. In a separate low-latency InferenceX benchmark, Together AI’s compiler reached 1,205 tokens per second while running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

signals.title: Open Agent Memory: persistent agent memory with sources you can inspect - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Open Agent Memory (OAM) is an Apache-2.0, self-hosted memory engine for AI agents. It retains eligible conversations, derives source-backed facts and Insights, and returns relevant evidence with citations. Your agent remains responsible for the final answer.

The v0.0.1 source and release are public, with a PostgreSQL/pgvector deployment, a bundled Memory Inspector, HTTP/OpenAPI integration, and OpenClaw and DeepSeek Harness plugins.

...

OAM's first-use path is: 

```
retain an eligible conversation
    -> receive an operation receipt
    -> wait for indexing readiness
    -> recall relevant evidence in a new session
    -> give that evidence to the agent
    -> inspect the original source

```

A successful retain response means the source and receipt were accepted. It does not mean indexing has finished. That distinction matters when wiring memory into a real application.

...

OAM is useful to evaluate when you want control over persistent memory, model bindings and source inspection in an existing agent. It is a memory engine rather than a hosted assistant or a replacement for the host's planning and answer logic.

Self-hosted storage does not mean all inference stays local: that depends on the endpoints you configure. Indexing and explicit Profile refresh can incur provider charges. The deployment has operational prerequisites, and the published local application-replica checks do not establish database high availability or physical multi-host resilience.

signals.title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation.

...

NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) splits one GPU into as many as seven instances, depending on the GPU. Each instance has its own compute, cache, memory and memory bandwidth. Because the split is in hardware rather than software, you get guarantees that other sharing methods can’t give:

1. Predictable latency – Each partition has dedicated memory bandwidth, so one model’s traffic spike doesn’t show up in another model’s p99.
2. Fault isolation – A crash or memory error stays inside its partition instead of taking down every model on the GPU.
3. Right-sized capacity – Small and mid-sized models get a slice that fits them instead of a whole GPU. You can mix slice sizes on one device.
4. No cold starts – Every model keeps its own partition and stays loaded, with no load penalty and no eviction.
5. Tenant isolation – Memory protection between partitions is enforced in hardware, which makes security and compliance reviews simpler.
6. Reliable planning and chargeback – A partition performs the same way regardless of its neighbors, so load tests predict production. GPU cost also maps cleanly to a model, team or tenant.

...

Four things stand out.

- The partition is faster everywhere – It delivered more output tokens per second in every scenario at every concurrency, by 53 percent to 89 percent at the load where each scenario’s cost benefit is largest, and lower inter-token latency in every one too, by 8.9 percent to 42.1 percent. The gap widens with load.
- Time to first token is lower in every case, by 5.6 percent to 47.5 percent.
- On cost it’s 18–34 percent cheaper per million output tokens, above a crossover that moves earlier as prompts lengthen. Concurrency 64 for 100-token prompts, 4 for 8,000-token prompts. Below the crossover the whole A100 is the cheaper unit. These prices are all on-demand, which at the time of analysis were measured as $25.251286 per hour for an `ml.p4d.24xlarge` and $63.296000 per hour for an `ml.p5.48xlarge` in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Purely for our own analysis, we derived the unit cost by dividing the whole-instance cost by the number of units on it: 8 on the p4d, and 16 on the p5, where our partition is half of a GPU.
- At the top of the ladder on long-context traffic, the A100 stopped serving. On both the 6,000- and 8,000-token workloads it failed a third to a half of its requests against a serving-path deadline, while the partition failed none. That is why those two panels end earlier than the rest.

signals.title: Zyphra introduces ZYFA : FlashAttention FP8 for AMD MI355X, up to 1.76x faster
signals.excerpt:
# Zyphra introduces ZYFA : FlashAttention FP8 for AMD MI355X, up to 1.76x faster

November 7, 2026

AI / news

Zyphra has released ZYFA (Zyphra FlashAttention on AMD), a set of FP8 and BF16 attention compute kernels designed for AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs. According to the company, its FP8 kernels are between 1.16 and 1.76 times faster than AITER, AMD’s default kernel library, on real model activations. The code is released as open source under the Apache 2.0 license.

- Zyphra released ZYFA, an open-source set of FP8 and BF16 attention kernels for AMD MI355X GPUs.
- Its FP8 kernels run 1.16 to 1.76 times faster than AMD’s AITER on real model activations.
- Lean P, ping-pong scheduling and block scaling overlap softmax work with matrix work to close the bottleneck.
- ZYFA handles only causal forward-pass prefill and works only on MI355X.

ZYFA is an FP8 attention engine designed for the prefill phase, i.e., processing the provided context ... It powers the Zyphra Optimization Engine (ZOE), which runs Zyphra Cloud. The BF16 kernels are written in HIP, while the FP8 kernels are hand-scheduled assembly code, produced by a generator written in Python.

...

On real activations at 16K, FP8 gains reach 1.16x for Mistral-7B, 1.17x for Qwen3-8B, and 1.76x for DeepSeek-V2-Lite. On Gaussian benchmarks at 32K, the FP8 kernel with head dimension 128 achieves 2,672 TFLOP/s, compared to 1,944 for AITER. The kernel also leads on the MLA form, with 2,464 TFLOP/s versus 1,237, a ratio of 1.99.

The gap between benchmarks and real models is due to the MI355X frequency, which depends on the number of bits toggling in the operands. AITER allows more small probabilities to become zeros or subnormal numbers, which toggles fewer bits and enables a higher clock: 2,108 MHz versus 1,628 MHz for ZYFA on the Mistral-7B layer. ZYFA nevertheless requires fewer total cycles. According to the Zyphra team, performance should be measured on real activations, at sustained frequency.

Compared to an fp64 calculation, ZYFA’s FP8 error is 0.22 times that of AITER on Mistral-7B and 0.38 times on Qwen3-8B. On the full Mistral-7B model, the KL divergence, which measures the difference between two probability distributions, reaches 3.4×10⁻³ with ZYFA and 5.9×10⁻³ with AITER. Zyphra also notes that ZYFA is limited to causal forward-pass prefill, without decoding or paged KV cache, and that it only works on MI355X.

signals.title: ROCm InferaSim: Cut LLM Serving Trial Costs and Deploy the Best Configuration
signals.excerpt:
# ROCm InferaSim: Cut LLM Serving Trial Costs and Deploy the Best Configuration

...

# ROCm InferaSim: Cut LLM Serving Trial Costs and Deploy the Best Configuration #

November 06, 2026 by Anshu Raina, Yao Fu, Zhang Jiejing, Peyman Razaghi, Shiksha Patel, Ravi Gupta, Deval Shah, Adeem Jassani, Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury, Lorri Rao, Kailash Gogineni, Zhenyu Gu, Onil Gunawardana, Emad Barsoum.

12 min read. | 3042 total words.

Software tools & optimizations

AI/ML, LLM, Optimization, Performance

AI

Serving an LLM well means making a lot of choices before you know the answer. You pick an engine, a parallel layout, precisions and scheduler settings, and for disaggregated serving a split between prefill and decode. That leaves thousands of candidates, and each trial ties up one or more multi-GPU nodes for minutes. Measuring every candidate in our searches would take about 25,000 GPU-hours, so most teams try a few guesses and keep the best. A guess that misses costs you extra GPUs or a missed latency target.

ROCm InferaSim replaces most of those measurements with fast projection. It measures once per set of kernels, calculates every configuration that runs them, and an agent searches the projections instead of the hardware. Each projection takes under half a second on one CPU core. On our own AMD Instinct™ MI355X runs, 11 anchors cost 9.1 GPU-hours and cover 226 configurations that took 204 GPU-hours to measure. GPU hours go to confirming a short list. The full method and evaluation are in the InferaSim paper [1].

...

- Fixed-length traffic, our runs: 8.1% median error on TPOT, 8.8% on throughput and 13.6% on TTFT over 172 configurations of eight models, from 11 anchors.
- Agentic multi-turn traffic, InferenceX AgentX runs: within about 8% on throughput, 14% on ITL and 23% on TTFT over 95 held-out configurations of six models, from 28 anchors.
- Disaggregated serving, InferenceX runs: 5.5% on throughput per GPU and 5.3% on interactivity over 159 deployments of 8–24 GPUs, with no disaggregated anchor. For four models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GLM-5, MiniMax-M3 and Qwen3.5-397B), InferaSim picks the right winner between disaggregation and colocation in 19 of 21 latency-tier decisions at 1k/1k and 23 of 27 at 8k/1k.
- Speculative decoding: on 43 measured MTP runs, within 12.2% on interactivity and 8.9% on throughput per GPU.
- Pipelines, our runs: SGLang at PP 1–8 is within 2.3–9.2% on TPOT, and two-node pipelines within 11.6%.
- Ranking: anchored mode orders 93.4% of decisive throughput pairs correctly, and simulate mode, with no measurement, 89.0%.

signals.title: Harness adapters: Safe RL for efficient agentic development
signals.excerpt:
# Harness adapters: Safe RL for efficient agentic development 

Published November 6, 2026 

Small LoRA adapters, trained with reinforcement learning inside pi, opencode and hermes, all served from one model, with every tool call the model makes inspected by safeagents before it runs. Follow the training runs on the live dashboard.

## In short 

- We release several "harness adapters". It is one LoRA adapter per model and harness, trained with RL on verifiable tasks, inside unmodified agent harnesses (pi, opencode and hermes).
- Harness adapters can make local agentic development more efficient and accurate. On held-out eval tasks, in our smoke training tests, they make fewer tool calls than the base model, while keeping or improving its accuracy.
- New environments come from open coding sessions shared on the Hub: Repo2RLEnvs turns them into verifiable tasks, mixed in training with SmolDataEnvs.
- safeagents, a proxy between the harness and the model, checks every tool call with rule-based detectors. Reward-hacking attempts are blocked and score 0.
- TwIL-8B, a reasoning model never trained as an agent, learns too. The final runs are streamed live.

...

### LoRA is the natural candidate for harness adapters 

LoRA adapters are cost-efficient for training and evaluation, since one server can host every harness's policy at once. At inference, anyone can load the adapter for the harness of their choice, to make the base model more efficient on their use case. We detail in One base model, many adapters how exactly we leverage LoRA adapters for training and evaluation.

...

safeagents is a reverse proxy: a small server placed in front of another one, that clients talk to as if it were the real thing. The harness's base URL points at safeagents instead of vLLM. Each request goes through unchanged; each response comes back through it, and the tool calls in it are checked before the harness sees them. Neither the harness nor vLLM knows it's there, and it speaks both the OpenAI Chat Completions and the Anthropic Messages APIs, streaming or not. In training, it runs on a background thread of the trainer.

signals.title: The Complete Guide to RAG, MCP, LangGraph, Embeddings, and Beyond - DEV Community
signals.excerpt:
Shipping a reliable, secure, and cost-effective production system requires mastering the Modern AI Stack. This ecosystem is not a single monolithic API; it is a distributed architecture of probabilistic reasoning engines (LLMs), semantic memory (Embeddings and Vector Databases), retrieval pipelines (RAG), orchestration layers (LangGraph, n8n), ... This guide maps the engineering reality of these technologies, distinguishing between open-weight models and hosted APIs, deterministic workflows and autonomous agents, and free developer tools versus enterprise-grade infrastructure.

...

- Parameters and Tokens: Parameters are the internal variables (weights and biases) the model adjusts during training. Models do not read words; they read tokens (sub-word chunks generated by algorithms like Byte-Pair Encoding). The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can hold in its active working memory.
- Fine-Tuning vs. RAG: Fine-tuning involves additional training on a specific dataset to alter the model's base weights. It is for teaching behavior, tone, or format.

...

- Quantization: The process of reducing the precision of model weights (e.g., from 16-bit floating point to 4-bit integers) to drastically reduce VRAM requirements and hardware costs, with minimal degradation to reasoning quality.
- Open-Weight vs. Open-Source: A crucial distinction.

...

## 6. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Agentic RAG 

LLMs suffer from knowledge cutoffs and hallucinations regarding private data. RAG solves this by retrieving relevant context from a vector database and injecting it into the LLM's prompt before generation.

### The RAG Pipeline 

1. Ingestion & Parsing: Extracting text from PDFs, HTML, or DOCX files.
2. Chunking: Splitting documents into semantic or fixed-size blocks. Poor chunking destroys context.
3. Metadata Extraction: Tagging chunks with source URLs, dates, and author data.
4. Embedding & Storage: Converting chunks to vectors and saving them in the DB.
5. Retrieval: Searching the DB with the user's query.
6. Reranking: Using a Cross-Encoder model to score the top 50 retrieved chunks and select the absolute best 5 for the prompt.
7. Generation: The LLM answers using only the provided context.

Common RAG Mistakes: Missing authorization filters (User A retrieves User B's private document chunks), and failing to evaluate retrieval separately from answer quality. More context does not automatically produce better answers; irrelevant context confuses the model and increases token costs.

### Agentic RAG vs. Traditional RAG 

Not all RAG systems are agents. 

- Traditional RAG: A deterministic pipeline. User asks a question -> System retrieves 5 chunks -> LLM generates an answer. 
- Agentic RAG: The LLM acts as an autonomous router. It analyzes the user's intent, decides which database to query, evaluates the returned data, and if the evidence is insufficient, it autonomously rewrites the query and searches again. 

Agentic RAG solves complex, multi-hop questions. However, iterative retrieval introduces severe trade-offs: multiplied latency, exponential token costs, and the risk of the agent entering an infinite loop of useless searches.

## 7. AI Agents, LangChain, and LangGraph 

An AI agent is an LLM embedded inside an execution loop with access to memory and external tools. An LLM is not necessarily an AI agent, and an AI agent is not simply a chatbot with a system prompt. 

- Chatbot: Waits for user input, generates text.
- Automated Workflow: Follows a rigid, deterministic DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) defined by a developer. An automated workflow is not automatically an agent.
- AI Agent: Given a high-level goal, it plans a sequence of steps, executes tools, observes the results, handles errors, and decides when the goal is achieved.

...

### LangChain vs. LangGraph 

LangChain and LangGraph are frequently confused, but they serve fundamentally different architectural purposes. LangChain and LangGraph should not be treated as identical technologies.

- LangChain: A library of integrations. It provides document loaders, vector store connectors, and basic chain abstractions. It relies on DAGs and struggles with complex loops or long-running state persistence.
- LangGraph: A state-machine orchestration engine built on top of LangChain concepts. It models your application as a cyclic graph of Nodes and Edges. It maintains persistent state, allows agents to loop and self-correct, and supports checkpointing (pausing execution for human approval and resuming days later).

Decision Matrix: If your application is a straight line from Input -> Retrieve -> Generate, use basic code or LangChain. If your application requires loops, branching logic, error recovery, and human oversight, you must use LangGraph.

signals.title: Unsloth Boosts Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Efficiency with New Dynamic V3.1 GGUF Quantizations | Tech Pulse | TheNextGenTechInsider
signals.excerpt:
# Unsloth Boosts Qwen3.8-Flash-Next Efficiency with New Dynamic V3.1 GGUF Quantizations

Unsloth has launched Dynamic v3.1 GGUF quantizations for the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model. This update improves accuracy by up to 15% and increases inference speed while optimizing memory usage for local deployment.

...

## Unsloth Releases Dynamic V3.1 GGUFs for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next

Unsloth has released its new Dynamic v3.1 GGUF quantizations for the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model, according to the developer's announcement. This update introduces significant improvements in accuracy and inference efficiency for local deployment of large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models.

The release is technically significant because it optimizes the 125B parameter Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model—which features 6B activated parameters and a 256K context window—for memory-constrained environments as detailed in the Hugging Face repository. By utilizing the Dynamic v3.1 algorithm, these quants aim to maintain high reasoning capabilities while reducing the computational overhead typically associated with frontier-scale models.

## Technical Implementation

The update introduces several key technical advancements:

- Engram Switching: A new process allows users to "mix and match" engram components across different precisions, such as BF16, Q8 0, Q5 1, and IQ4_NL as described in the Unsloth documentation. This enables developers to swap table shards to optimize the balance between disk space and precision.
- Precision Metrics: The relative Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) compared to BF16 is notably low across formats: 0.0053 for Q8 0, 0.0376 for Q5 1, and 0.0757 for IQ4_NL according to the technical specifications.
- Hardware Scaling: The model's requirements scale based on quantization, ranging from 32GB of RAM for the smallest 1-bit version to 355GB for BF16 as noted in the Unsloth usage guide.

## Performance Results

The Dynamic v3.1 quants demonstrate superior performance compared to previous GSQ-RCO versions and other frontier quants of similar size as reported in the Unsloth technical notes:

- Accuracy: A 10-15% increase in accuracy on benchmarks including DeepSWE, Terminal Bench, and Aider Polyglot.
- Efficiency: Up to 50% reduction in token usage and a 7% increase in inference speed as documented in the Hugging Face release notes.
- Benchmark Validation: Results were verified through 26.2B tokens of benchmarking, including 18.1B tokens for DeepSWE and 5.2B for Terminal Bench.

...

The new GGUF files are currently available for download via the Unsloth Hugging Face repository.

signals.title: Tencent DSpine draft model reaches up to 3.84× AR throughput
signals.excerpt:
# Tencent releases DSpine draft model for Qwen3.8-27B, reporting up to 3.84× faster agent decoding

Tencent released a five-layer DSpine draft model for Qwen3.8-27B that uses parallel drafting with adjacent causal injection. It reached up to 3.84× autoregressive decoding throughput on agent benchmarks in SGLang tests.

...

Tencent has released a new speculative decoding draft model called DSpine for the Qwen3.8-27B large language model, claiming up to 3.84× speedup over autoregressive decoding on agent-style workloads. The five-layer draft model, published on Hugging Face as tencent/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16, drafts in blocks of 16 tokens with an 8,192-token sliding window. Qwen3.8-27B itself is the dense 27-billion-parameter model in Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 open-model family and has been on Hugging Face since August.

...

Benchmarks published on the Hugging Face model card show DSpine outperforming DFlash2 across general and agent benchmarks. On general reasoning tasks at temperature 0, DSpine achieves acceptance lengths of 7.20 on GSM8K versus 5.69 for DFlash2, 6.49 versus 5.49 on MATH-500, and 5.71 versus 4.87 on HumanEval. At temperature 1, the gaps narrow but persist: 6.31 versus 5.45 on GSM8K and 5.66 versus 5.27 on MATH-500.

On agent benchmarks — WorkBuddy Code, Web, Office, SWE-bench Pro, and τ²-bench — DSpine shows consistent acceptance-length gains over DFlash2 at both low and xhigh reasoning settings. End-to-end throughput measurements in SGLang 0.5.22 with BF16, FlashAttention 3, and concurrency 8 show DSpine reaching 686.23 tokens/s (2.71× speedup over AR) on WorkBuddy Code at low reasoning, and 840.14 tokens/s (3.33×) on WorkBuddy Web at xhigh reasoning. The draft model uses DSpark-based dynamic verification with ReplaySSM enabled.

Tencent’s serving recipe uses SGLang with a specific configuration, including linear attention backend Triton, Mamba SSM dtype float32, and a max mamba cache size of 64. Its example launch command sets a 131,072-token context and up to eight concurrent requests. The repository’s changelog dates the paper, the inference code, the Qwen3-8B draft weights and the training code (in SpecForge) to October 2026, and Qwen3.8-27B inference support and Apple Silicon inference via mlx-lm and SGLang-MLX to November. The authors are from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Tencent YouTu Lab and Xiamen University.

- General benchmark acceptance length gains over DFlash2 at T=0: GSM8K 7.20 vs 5.69, MATH-500 6.49 vs 5.49, HumanEval 5.71 vs 4.87, MBPP 6.14 vs 5.04, MT-Bench 4.48 vs 4.11

signals.title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Artificial Intelligence
signals.excerpt:
Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves.

...

You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent.

...

Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result.

Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back:

- A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available.
- Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information.
- Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads pages to verify facts, and decides when it has enough evidence to answer.
- Responsible AI safeguards: Web Answer is designed and tested with responsible AI safeguards.

...

Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model:

- Web Search: Returns ranked URLs, titles, snippets, and metadata. You keep your own model and control the synthesis. Use Web Search when you want full control over how results are processed.
- Web Answer: Runs the model, the agentic retrieval loop, synthesis, and attribution for you. You get a finished, cited answer. Use Web Answer when the question is a sub-task inside a larger agent and you do not want to own a retrieval pipeline for it.

Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer.

signals.title: Intel offers Day-0 dupport for Meta's Muse Spark open data center silicon built for 816B scale
signals.excerpt:
Meta’s official open-weight release of Muse Spark Open, an 816 billion-parameter any-to-text model, represents a major milestone in multimodal AI and the most capable U.S. open-weights model released to date.

Deploying an 816 billion-parameter architecture requires extreme memory efficiency and hardware-level low-precision acceleration. Intel has enabled day-0 support across Intel Xeon® processors and Intel data center GPU platforms, Intel GPU D-series, through targeted low-bit model quantization.

...

Muse Spark Open has been tested and is running on the upcoming Intel GPU D-series, today. This early work reflects Intel’s commitment to day-0 support for emerging AI models and gives customers an early path to begin evaluating Muse Spark Open on Intel silicon.

Muse Spark Open inference was running on four Intel GPU D-series GPUs. Each GPU provides 160 GB of memory, offering sufficient capacity to run Muse Spark Open across four GPUs.

...

Muse Spark Open on Intel Xeon processors Designed for high-capacity CPU inference, Intel Xeon processors support INT4 weight-only quantized (WOQ) inference, reducing memory footprint, while leveraging Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel AMX) to accelerate AI matrix operations.

...

Software support and enablement Intel’s Upstreaming First software strategy helps enterprise AI engineering teams deploy both quantized variants using standard open-source tools.

Full upstream support for compressed tensors, such as MXFP4, and GPTQ (INT4 WOQ) in mainline vLLM enables hardware-accelerated matrix execution, continuous batching and PagedAttention across multinode deployments. Native upstream integration for microscaling (MX) execution and Intel XPU-optimized kernels in SGLang drives high-throughput continuous batching and low-bit inference for complex, multiturn agentic workflows.

To maximize efficiency on Intel silicon without sacrificing accuracy, Intel quantized MXFP4 and INT4 variants directly from Muse Spark Open’s original BF16 weights using vLLM’s native quantization tool, llm-compressor, powered by the AutoRound quantization algorithm.

Intel’s AutoRound algorithm optimizes rounding and clipping-range parameters layer by layer, helping preserve Muse Spark Open’s fine-grained reasoning capabilities even at ultra-low bit widths.

The MXFP4 weights, in compressed-tensors format, target Intel GPU D-series GPUs to use native hardware acceleration, while the INT4 weights, in GPTQ format, support Xeon processors in weight-only quantization mode to minimize memory footprint and latency.

signals.excerpt:

# Introducing AgentEnv: An Open-Source Framework for Building RL Environments

By Edgar Arakelyan, Tejas Polakam, Yzabelle Go

An agent is only as good as the world it operates in, and building worlds that are realistic, accurate, and scalable all at once is the hard part of scaling RL. Every RL environment Scale builds runs on AgentEnv. Today we're open-sourcing it.

...

AgentEnv’s philosophy starts from the world first, so one Environment can host many Tasks and many agents.

...

Building blocks: What an Environment is made of. An Environment is built from versioned composable blocks: Environments like Slack or Gmail, an Artifact of data that populates them, and Rules (the clock, triggers, and roles) that govern how it behaves.

Interoperability: What an Environment works with. An Environment doesn't assume anything about who or what runs it. Any agent can connect to it, any sandbox can host it, and your cloud can run it, all through open protocols instead of custom glue.

...

Agent Agnostic. An Environment's card tells an agent which tools it serves and how to reach them, over MCP, REST or a generated CLI. An agent's Agent Card, from the open A2A protocol, does the same in the other direction.

Pair any Environment Card with any Agent Card and the agent can start work, with no custom wiring. The same Task runs unchanged and consistent on Claude Code, OpenAI's agents, or any of your own custom agents.

...

### What comes out of the box

AgentEnv ships 48 built-in step types, covering everything from deploying an Environment to setting its Rules of the World to grading trajectories. Most RL Tasks can be built from these alone, with no new code. For the rest, you can add your own steps as plugins.

# zml/llmd 20261106.0

More models, less waiting.

 November 6, 2026 inference / serving / NVIDIA / AMD / TPU / Metal / Intel 

We are pleased to announce the release of `zml/llmd 20261106.0`. This week, we are bringing two new models, asynchronous scheduling in beta, and more performance work across our backends.

...

We have added asynchronous scheduling to Llama and Gemma 4. The idea is simple: while the accelerator is running one step, the CPU can prepare the next one. Less time waiting between steps.

You can enable it with `--async-scheduling`. It is opt-in for now. Speculative decoding still uses the synchronous path, and Llama’s asynchronous path also works with data parallelism. The next release should bring more models on board.

...

# Data parallelism beta

Llama now supports `--data-parallel`. This distributes requests and their KV caches across groups of devices. We also improved weight sharding for this configuration to reduce communication between those groups.

For example, `--data-parallel=2` splits the work across two groups.

On 2×RTX 5090, our Llama development benchmark went from 700 to 1,600 tok/s with `--data-parallel=2`, `--batch-size=16` and `--token-batch-size=256`. That’s a 2.3× improvement to the data-parallel path. The same benchmark with `--data-parallel=1` stays at roughly 2,000 tok/s, so the best configuration still depends on the workload.

...

# Faster prefill

The hill climb continues. This week, we worked on Gated DeltaNet, with new CuTe kernels for NVIDIA and Fly kernels for AMD. The NVIDIA and AMD implementations improve prefill performance over the previous Triton backend.

signals.title: Agents Are Going Async
signals.excerpt:
## Key Takeaways

- As agents take on bigger goals, they need to stay responsive to the user while making progress on many long tasks at once.
- Async subagents split an agent into an orchestrator that stays available to the user and subagents that run tasks in the background and report back to the orchestrator upon completion.
- Background work is becoming the norm for agent infrastructure, from coding agents like Claude Code to personal agents like OpenAI's dots.

...

We’re bringing this pattern to Deep Agents with async subagents. An orchestrator stays available to the user and keeps the conversation's context organized, while async subagents run as background workers and report back when they finish. The amount of work the agent can take on then grows with the number of background workers instead of the length of one loop.

...

An agent runs in a loop. The model calls a tool, waits for the result, and decides what to do next. Historically, tools and subagents blocked that loop until they returned, like code that awaits each slow call in turn. An async subagent works like a task started with `asyncio.create_task` or a `Promise` you don't await yet. The call returns right away, the work runs independently in the background, and the result comes back later.

...

Async subagents are available in Deep Agents for Python and JavaScript, and in Managed Deep Agents, where making a subagent async takes one field:

```python
from managed_deepagents import define_deep_agent

agent = define_deep_agent(
    name="research-assistant",
    model="openai:gpt-5.5",
    subagents=[
        {
            "name": "researcher",
            "description": "Researches a topic in the background.",
            "system_prompt": "Research the topic and report your findings.",
            "async": True,
        },
    ],
)
```

signals.title: Google Open-Sources the Engine Behind Its Biggest Products - GEroundtable
signals.excerpt:
On 5 November, Google open-sourced the inference engine that already answers more than six million queries every second inside its own products. XLA Serving Engine, a C++ runtime for the OpenXLA ecosystem, moves machine-learning models out of Python and into production serving, and Google says it powers YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, Search and parts of Gemini Omni. The release turns a year of internal production use into public infrastructure anyone can now run.

...

Most machine-learning engineers train models in Python, using frameworks such as JAX and PyTorch, but many production environments refuse Python because of its deployment and operational complexity. XLA Serving Engine bridges that gap with what Google calls a “Train in Python, Serve in C++” workflow, exporting a model into a compiled format that a native C++ runtime can execute directly.

The export format is an XLA SavedModel, which stores the model’s computation as StableHLO, a portable intermediate representation, while Orbax checkpointing stores the weights. Once exported, the XLA Serving Runtime loads the artifact, wraps the PJRT execution interface directly, and applies the XLA compiler’s optimisations, cutting out the Python interpreter and its global interpreter lock entirely.

...

For short requests, Google reports that the engine delivers two to five times the throughput of the best Python server its team could build, and eight to thirty-six times that of a straightforward one. It uses thirty to seventy percent less CPU time per prediction and roughly a quarter of the memory, though these are Google’s measurements and remain unverified.

Scale is the stronger claim. Google began deploying core components of the engine in its internal production infrastructure last year, and it now serves over six million queries per second. Google names YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, Search and parts of Gemini Omni among the products it serves — proven infrastructure, not a laboratory prototype.

...

Google is candid about the engine’s limits. It is a lightweight, one-shot inference engine, and for large autoregressive language models with long context lengths, the company recommends established projects such as vLLM or SGLang, which handle LLM-specific memory management. The engine is aimed at vision, embedding and recommendation models rather than chatbots.

Google plans TorchTPU integration so PyTorch users can export models to the same format and serve them on TPUs in C++, plus ahead-of-time compilation to cut cold-start times and a C++ data preprocessor for teams wanting preprocessing inside the model graph. Docker images tested on CPU, GPU and TPU, with simple gRPC APIs, are available now.

signals.title: Box Taps Nvidia Nemotron for Agent-First Content Retrieval | AI Weekly
signals.excerpt:
## TL;DR

- Box Content Retrieval uses Nvidia's Nemotron embeddings so AI agents can pull relevant document chunks instead of reading whole files.
- Nvidia's Kari Briski says the system delivers queries four times faster, with 20% fewer errors and 90% fewer tokens used.
- The feature rolls out to Box Enterprise Advance customers early next year, announced at Box's developer conference on Nov 5, 2026.

...

Box used its developer conference on Nov 5 to unveil Content Retrieval, a new system that plugs Nvidia's Nemotron embeddings into Box so enterprise AI agents can pull the most relevant chunks of a document instead of ingesting the whole file. TechCrunch reported the integration, with the performance numbers attributed to Nvidia rather than an independent benchmark.

The headline claim, from Nvidia VP of generative AI software Kari Briski, is that the setup lets "queries to be answered four times faster, with 20% fewer errors and 90% fewer tokens used." Box CEO Aaron Levie framed the point in plainer terms: "Instead of an agent having to kind of read through each document, we can send back chunks from the documents that are most relevant to the user's query or whatever the task is that the agent is doing." He also described the product as a bundle, saying Box is "probably packing in five different technologies into one simple API."

Box says Content Retrieval will be available to all Enterprise Advance customers, rolling out early next year. It lands in a busy stretch of enterprise-agent news on our radar, alongside this week's Sierra/Anon acquisition — part of a run of enterprise AI coverage where retrieval and agent action are increasingly sold as one layer.
